summary: American and Saudi fighter aircraft struck logistics and weapons sites in eastern Iraq on Wednesday, targeting Iran-backed militias in response to a prior Iranian missile barrage against American forces.

Retaliatory strikes began Wednesday evening following Iran's missile launch at American forces in the Middle East , which U.S. Central Command described as a "powerful response" to the attempted attack.
The Popular Mobilization Forces reported at least 20 fighters killed and 32 wounded in the overnight strikes, while six Iranian advisers died and Jordan intercepted five Iranian missiles.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi indefinitely postponed his visit to Saudi Arabia on Thursday, while Brent crude prices jumped 7.3% amid concerns over regional energy stability.
Global energy supply chains face potential threats as investors monitor the Middle East, though Saudi officials warned they do not seek escalation despite the military response.
title: Source Icon

Right-Leaning coverage, by contrast, centers procedural accountability, stressing that Cornyn and Tillis made “demands,” the vote was “postpones/stalled,” and DOJ had not produced written proposals, while phrasing like “JUST IN” adds urgency.

summary: On Thursday, the Senate Judiciary Committee delayed its planned vote on acting Attorney General Blanche's nomination after Republican holdouts led by Sen. John Cornyn demanded changes to a controversial Justice Department settlement.
Cornyn pushed the DOJ to clarify audit immunity terms in a $1.8 billion settlement that Blanche brokered to resolve President Donald Trump 's $10 billion suit against the Internal Revenue Service.

Survivor Dani Bensky testified this month that the DOJ's release of Jeffrey Epstein–related files retraumatized victims, citing exposure of more than 100 victims' identifying information and nude images.
Senators agreed Wednesday via unanimous consent to a nonbinding resolution opposing clemency for Ghislaine Maxwell, with Sen. Jacky Rosen calling it a signal ahead of the Blanche vote.
The committee vote is not decisive; Blanche could proceed to a floor vote or continue serving as acting attorney general for many months, depending on Senate Republican leadership.
title: Judiciary Committee cancels vote on Blanche AG nomination amid GOP opposition

summary: On Wednesday, July 29, 2026, a jury convicted Hadi Matar of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie , exposing him to a potential life sentence.
Matar stabbed Rushdie 15 times in August 2022 at the Chautauqua Institution, acting on a decades-old death threat tied to the author's 1988 novel, The Satanic Verses.
Digital records from 2021 and 2022 show Matar tracking Rushdie's public appearances and messaging contacts that he "wanted everyone to know he was doing this for Hezbollah."

Already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence for attempted murder, Matar faces additional federal penalties after declining to testify; defense lawyer Nathaniel Barone argued the government lacked proof of intent.
An Iranian foundation maintains a bounty of more than $3 million for killing Rushdie, yet the author published a 2024 memoir and returned to fiction with last year's The Eleventh Hour.
title: Man convicted in terrorism trial over the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie

The central line is more procedural, balancing the Fed’s dual mandate and “no magic wand” limits.
Both sides agree inflation is above target and the vote split matters, but they diverge on whether the story is policy caution or a leadership crisis.
summary: The Federal Open Market Committee voted 9-3 on Wednesday to maintain the federal funds rate between 3.5% and 3.75%, marking the fifth consecutive hold despite internal pressure for higher rates.

Persistent inflation has remained above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, while conflict in the Middle East adds economic uncertainty, though officials noted that activity expands at a solid pace.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan dissented, preferring a quarter-point increase as they have been most explicit about the need for higher rates.
Markets largely expected the hold, though 76% of traders now foresee a rate hike in September; New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declared he has "no tolerance" for elevated inflation.

Bank of America analysts expect three quarter-point hikes this year, potentially reaching 4.25% to 4.5%, as policymakers await Thursday's Commerce Department data on economic growth and inflation measures.
title: Fed Holds Rates Steady, Three Officials Dissent Favoring a Hike

summary: Former NIAID Director Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination during a Senate hearing investigating the origins of COVID-19, declining to answer questions from lawmakers.

Fauci accused Committee Chair Sen. Rand Paul of an "unhinged obsession" with trying to put him "behind bars," arguing in his opening statement that the hearing was orchestrated solely to entrap him into legal jeopardy.

The confrontation follows Sen. Paul's weekend release of over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary, which contained entries detailing early pandemic discussions regarding the lab-leak hypothesis and NIH research grants.
Tensions flared further when Sen. Paul ordered Capitol Police to escort Fauci's attorney out of the room after a dispute over committee procedures and legal representation speaking rights.

Sen. Paul maintained that the American public is owed an apology, reiterating allegations that Fauci misled Congress and downplayed theories that SARS-CoV-2 originated from U.S.-funded research in Wuhan, China.
title: Anthony Fauci invokes 5th Amendment right not to testify at Covid hearing, calls Sen. Rand Paul ‘unhinged’

summary: On Tuesday, the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton, President Donald Trump 's pick to lead the intelligence community, in a 51-47 vote, ending Bill Pulte's 40-day tenure as acting Director.

Pulte, a housing executive with no national security experience, implemented staffing cuts that cumulatively axed approximately 30% of staff while focusing on declassifying 2020 election documents at the President's request.

During a hearing two weeks ago, Clayton refused to say Joe Biden won the 2020 election, testifying it was "certified," prompting Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer to call his performance "abysmal."
Clayton inherits an office described as "severely understaffed" with "deeply degraded" authority, positioned as a "deep state" target by Trump amid historic institutional decline.
title: Senate confirms Jay Clayton as nation’s intelligence director

summary: On Wednesday, Pakistan security forces launched an operation in Swat's Matta tehsil, killing four terrorists; Elite Force Constable Gulfam was martyred while "bravely fighting the terrorists" on Tuesday night.

For several months, militants designated as Fitna-al-Khawarij have maintained presence in Swat's Kabal and Matta tehsils as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa faces escalating security challenges from terrorist groups.
Security sources confirmed four militants used residents as human shields inside a Matta house; forces secured the strategic Rashid Sar location during the ongoing clearance operation.
In Hangu district, militants attacked the Khazina Banda police check post Wednesday evening with heavy weapons, killing nine police personnel including DSP Diyar Khan and wounding 28 others.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi commended security forces as the "Azm-e-Istehkam" campaign intensifies, while Islamabad maintains Afghanistan's Taliban government provides sanctuary to TTP militants—allegations Kabul repeatedly denies.
title: Militants attack a Pakistani police post and kill 5 officers in a northwestern province

summary: On Wednesday, the U.S. Space Force awarded SpaceX $1.6 billion to launch 18 Falcon 9 missions from Vandenberg Space Force Base through 2027, supporting the military's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio.

Space Force acquisition official Eric Zarybnisky cited an "unprecedented two-month acquisition timeline," noting the service completed procurement from requirement identification to contract signature in roughly two months.

SpaceX remains the only company with necessary West Coast infrastructure and operational Falcon 9 rockets for this scale, while rivals United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin face ongoing technical investigations.

The satellites will support the Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, a key element of the Trump administration's proposed $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense initiative to track airborne threats.

Reflecting increased military demand, the Space Force raised the Phase 3 Lane 1 contract ceiling to $17 billion earlier this month, signaling expectations for substantially faster growth in national security launches.
title: SpaceX gets $1.6 billion US Space Force order for 18 Falcon 9 launches

summary: On Wednesday, Immigration and Customs Enforcement released witness Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego from detention following a federal judge's order, allowing him to reunite with family and visit the memorial at the shooting site.

ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo on July 7 during what ICE called a 'targeted enforcement operation' in Houston's East End; attorneys for the three passengers, including Pliego, have refuted ICE's account.
Federal Judge Keith Ellison ruled Monday that authorities must release Pliego within 48 hours in a public place, requiring officials to provide his counsel with three hours' notice beforehand.

Prosecutors filed a motion Wednesday to stay the release, citing the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals case Rodriguez v. Ortega to argue that precedent mandates Pliego's continued detention pending appeal.

Legal teams for the two other passengers have filed similar petitions for release, while advocacy group FIEL Houston demands protection for all witnesses, stating, 'We must do all we can to protect these key witnesses.
title: Witness to a fatal ICE shooting in Houston is released from immigration detention
topic_full: Immigration and Customs Enforcement · United States

summary: On Tuesday, Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti and Southeastern Conference officials began reviewing a revised Protect College Sports Act, facing a 9 a.m. Wednesday deadline to determine their support for the legislation.

Congressional sponsors introduced revisions to the Protect College Sports Act, aiming to secure Big Ten and SEC support by offering concessions on revenue sharing, conference realignment, and state law preemption.

Key changes include a new $25 million retention pool for athlete compensation and $5 million dedicated to women's sports, supplementing the $21.3 million schools currently spend annually on roster spending.
Petitti remains cautious, stating he must see if the bill 'provides a lot more help than not' before the Big Ten decides whether to support it alongside the SEC.
Uncertainty persists regarding the bill's path to the Senate floor, as Senate Majority Leader John Thune previously warned it is unlikely to reach a vote before the Aug 7 recess.
title: Senators still working with SEC, Big Ten on thorny issues involved in college sports bill

summary: On Wednesday, the Before Columbus Foundation named Stephen Colbert a recipient of the 47th annual American Book Awards, honoring him with the organization's 'anti-censorship' prize.
Established by author-playwright-publisher Ishmael Reed, the foundation created the awards to provide recognition for outstanding literary achievement from America's diverse community.

Alongside Colbert, independent bookseller Mitchell Kaplan of Coral Gables, Florida, and lifetime achievement prize winner Novelist-playwright Karen Tei Yamashita received honors; publishers Morgan Entrekin and Roger Malina also received awards.
CBS ended Colbert's 11-year run on The Late Show in May, removing a platform for one of Trump's critics, though Colbert and others have questioned the network's economic rationale.
Literary releases honored by the foundation range from Nicholas Boggs' Baldwin and John Fugelsang's Separation of Church and Hate to Adela Najarro's poetry collection Variations in Blue.
title: Stephen Colbert Wins an Anti-Censorship Award After CBS Ends 'The Late Show'

summary: On Tuesday, an independent report from Massachusetts-based Sanghavi Law Office detailed 70 firsthand accounts of sexual misconduct by 47 adults associated with Interlochen Center for the Arts, spanning the 1950s through the 2010s.
The Interlochen Board commissioned the review in 2024 following allegations against longtime music faculty member Byron Hanson, later expanding the scope to include financier Jeffrey Epstein .
Epstein, who donated more than $400,000 to the school, was accused of sexual contact by two alumni, while other firsthand accounts detailed grooming and assault by faculty and staff.

Interlochen President Trey Devey and Board Chair Barrett Rollins apologized for the "absolutely heartbreaking" abuse, stating the school provided names of the accused to the Grand Traverse County Prosecutor.

Declaring that "Interlochen today is fundamentally different," leadership noted that none of the 47 accused individuals remain employed and the school has implemented mandatory reporting and background checks.
title: Investigation Revealed 'Devastating' Reports of Sexual Misconduct at School Supported by Epstein

summary: A first-of-its-kind study published this week by the CDC suggests invasive mold infections are an underappreciated threat, with researchers identifying about 450 cases in Atlanta-area hospitals over five years.
While most people inhale mold spores without issue, they can be life-threatening to individuals with weakened immune systems, including cancer patients and those recovering from COVID-19.

Hospitals can expect to see 3 to 5 cases per year for every 100 inpatient beds, while CDC researchers previously estimated more than 15,000 hospitalizations annually tied to invasive mold disease in the United States.

CDC senior author Dr. Jeremy Gold said the data helps hospital administrators determine if case numbers represent an expected baseline or a potential outbreak, calling it "the first time we've had an estimate like this."

Duke University researcher Jeffrey Jenks said climate change may increase infection frequency. While Jenks called the findings "valuable," he noted studying different parts of the United States is necessary to understand regional generalizability.
title: Study suggests the threat of mold-associated illnesses may be underappreciated

summary: On Wednesday, the Caribbean Court ruled that U.S. extradition proceedings against Guyana opposition leader Azruddin Mohamed and his father, Nazar Mohamed, can resume after they challenged the request in Trinidad.

U.S. authorities indicted the Mohameds in Florida last year on allegations of smuggling more than 10,000 kilograms of gold and evading more than $50 million in taxes, though their defense argued some charges were not extraditable.

The Treasury Department sanctioned the duo for selling gold to buyers in Miami, Dubai, and the United Arab Emirates, while Azruddin Mohamed leads the second-largest party in Guyana's Parliament and founded the We Invest in Nationhood Party.

After the hearing, Nazar Mohamed told The Associated Press that "it is a 256-page judgement" and their attorneys are reviewing it, stating "Based on what lawyers say, all is not lost as yet. We will be fighting all the way."

While the extradition process resumes, the U.S. maintains friendly relations with the administration of President Irfaan Ali as the South American nation experiences an economic boom driven by offshore oil deposits that Venezuela has long claimed.
title: A Caribbean Court Rules that a US Extradition Process Against Guyana's Opposition Leader Can Resume

summary: On Wednesday, District Judge Royce Lamberth questioned the government's move to segregate transgender women in a Texas prison , citing concerns it violates his June injunction against President Donald Trump's executive order.

Trump's executive order last year directed the Bureau to house inmates by biological sex, but Lamberth previously enjoined part of this order, requiring officials to house plaintiffs in women's facilities.

Ten women are held in the Fort Worth unit, including four plaintiffs in the Washington case; attorney Alexander Shalom argued the "quasi-solitary unit" conditions exacerbate their gender dysphoria and violate constitutional protections.

Justice Department attorney Jared Littman argued the transfers comply because the judge didn't mandate housing with cisgender women, though Lamberth countered that segregating plaintiffs and depriving them of privileges violates the ruling "on its face".
The government intends to transfer all transgender inmates in the lawsuit to this unit, while Lamberth suggested the refusal to simply follow his directive appeared insubordinate.
title: Judge weighs bid to block or reverse transfers of transgender inmates into a segregated prison unit

summary: Howard University interim President Wayne Frederick announced Wednesday that more than 200 of the 502 students recently unenrolled have been reinstated, with the school working to resolve cases for remaining students before fall classes begin.

Last week, Howard sent 502 unenrollment notices to students whose accounts failed to reflect required financial or enrollment obligations, leaving many struggling to clarify requirements through communication channels.

Keana Johnson, a 17-year-old student living in a New York City shelter, was among those initially unenrolled but confirmed her reinstatement after traveling to campus with a staffer. "I feel great," Johnson told the AP.

Earlier this week, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul guaranteed admission to State University of New York and City University of New York campuses for affected residents, waiving the usual $800 enrollment deposit.

Defending the university's strict deadline enforcement as necessary for planning, Frederick pledged to expand communication efforts and provide earlier financial aid packages next year to prevent similar situations.
title: Howard U. interim president says more than 200 students reenrolled of 502 who received email

summary: On Thursday, Israeli strikes killed at least three people, including two children, in Khan Younis and Bureij refugee camp, health officials said. The Israeli military stated both strikes targeted Hamas militants.

The IDF continues operations despite the October 2025 ceasefire, which halted full-scale fighting but failed to end near-daily Israeli strikes. Gaza 's Health Ministry reports at least 1,209 Palestinians killed since the agreement began.

On Tuesday, Israeli forces destroyed a mosque and dozens of tents in Gaza City after ordering a forced evacuation. Medics reported the attack left many Palestinians without shelter, with wounded transported to Nasser Hospital.

Mediators from Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey held new talks with Hamas leaders on Thursday regarding the U.S.-brokered peace plan. A Hamas official described the group's response as "positive and good," though disarmament remains contested.

Israel effectively controls an estimated 64% of the Gaza Strip, where nearly all of Gaza's 2 million people live in makeshift tents or damaged buildings. This dominance underscores extreme humanitarian strain as mediation efforts continue.
title: Israeli Strikes in Gaza Kill at Least Two Palestinians

summary: Kuwait's military reported on Thursday that an Iranian strike hit a building belonging to a Chinese firm, killing one worker and causing severe damage in northern Kuwait.
The attack occurred after the United States military completed 'a heavy wave of strikes against Iran' in response to an earlier Iranian missile assault on a U.S. base in Jordan.

Jordan's air defenses intercepted five missiles launched from Iran Thursday morning, while U.S. Central Command stated the U.S. struck 'dozens' of targets belonging to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Elsewhere, British maritime security firm Ambrey reported drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta on Wednesday; Egypt's Petroleum Ministry confirmed no casualties.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman met with President Donald Trump and Vice President Vance on Wednesday to discuss de-escalation, as mediators remain 'still trying with both sides' to restore calm.
title: An Iranian Strike Has Hit a Chinese Firm's Building, Killing 1 Worker in Kuwait

summary: On July 30, Australia's internet regulator initiated Federal Court proceedings against Telegram , alleging the messaging platform failed to remove pro-terror videos and executions.

Commissioner Julie Inman Grant reported "five very difficult months of non-responsiveness" after her office first approached Telegram in March 2024 regarding transparency notices about extremist material.

The regulator alleges Telegram failed to remove known extremist content for up to three weeks, missing material linked to the Christchurch and Buffalo terror attacks amid warnings from ASIO Director General Mike Burgess.
Communications Minister Anika Wells stated the government has "no tolerance for big tech to fail," with Telegram facing civil penalties of up to A$54.6 million if the Federal Court finds breaches.
Founder Pavel Durov, based in Dubai, faces separate international legal challenges including Russian charges of facilitating terrorism and a prior August 2024 arrest in France.
title: Australia Begins Legal Action Against Telegram Over Alleged Pro-Terror Material

summary: On Wednesday, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced his office is opening an investigation into Anthony Fauci , citing the former health official's "lack of candor to Congress."

The investigation follows a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing where Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right over 100 times, while Sen. Rand Paul released over 1,000 pages of his diary.

Florida Republicans, including Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Rick Scott, criticized Fauci's pandemic handling. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna urged state officials to pursue charges, arguing that federal pardons do not shield Fauci from state-level prosecution.
Sen. Paul stated he will hold a vote next week on whether to declare Fauci in contempt of Congress, while Fauci maintained silence on legal advice fearing prosecution.

Although President Joe Biden granted Fauci an unconditional pardon in January 2025 for federal offenses, Uthmeier and other state officials maintain this does not prevent state-level investigations, leaving the pardon's scope a central legal question.
title: Florida AG launching investigation into Fauci after Senate hearing

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the story as an alarming example of an “obscure,” “secretive,” “dormant” court being used to test state power, stressing due process and deportation skepticism, while right-leaning coverage portrays the same move as Trump’s tough-on-terror enforcement, using sharper terms like “revives,” “never used,” “terror,” and “in the government’s sights.” The biggest dividing lines are the court’s novelty and the woman’s ISIS ties: left emphasis stays on procedural irregularity, right emphasis on security threat and crackdown.

summary: On Thursday, the Justice Department seeks to deport Nazira Haji Zada of Fort Worth, Texas, using the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, marking the first use of the obscure tribunal in 30 years.
An FBI memo dated July 15 alleges Nazira 'supported' an ISIS-inspired plot and had her children pledge loyalty to the Islamic State group, prompting her arrest earlier this week.
Court filings identify Nazira as mother and mother-in-law to two Afghan men convicted in Oklahoma for their roles in a 2024 Election Day plot targeting American voters.
Her son Abdullah Haji Zada received 15 years in prison last November, while son-in-law Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to the Islamic State group.
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche stated Congress created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court 30 years ago to remove 'alien terrorists' who 'never should have been here in the first place.
title: US uses dormant court to seek deportation of Afghan woman accused of aiding terror plot

The 15-year-old faces charges of assault with a firearm and unlawful gun possession, while a 19-year-old suspect was killed at the scene.

title: Police: Bullets that Killed 2 Bystanders at Seattle Festival Weren't From Teen Shooter's Gun

summary: On Wednesday, Dan Sohail was sentenced in federal court to time served plus seven days for intentionally damaging the Chabad-Lubavitch global headquarters in Crown Heights earlier this year.
Sohail, 36, drove his 2012 Honda Accord into the Eastern Parkway side entrance on Jan. 28 during a yahrtzeit gathering, later citing mental health challenges and icy conditions.
Driving into the building five times caused significant damage, though no one was injured among dozens inside. District Judge Eric Vitaliano ordered $19,010 in restitution for repairs.

Federal prosecutors sought a 14-month sentence arguing the act was a hate crime , but Judge Vitaliano rejected that characterization after reviewing psychiatric reports on Sohail's mental health struggles.
Prosecutors noted that 80 of 146 hate crime incidents in New York City this year targeted Jewish institutions, while defense attorney Mia Eisner-Grynberg called the act an "irrational cry for help.
title: Man gets 6-month sentence for ramming car into Jewish group’s NY world headquarters

summary: On Tuesday, singer Noah Kahan criticized the White House for using his song "American Cars" in a social media post depicting President Donald Trump's visit to a General Motors flagship test site in Michigan.

After fans tagged him, Kahan responded on Tuesday afternoon with disapproval: "Would never approve of my music being used in support of you or this administration." Co-writer Noah Levine added, "You fat fuck this song isn't for you."

While the track was removed from Instagram following the backlash, it remains featured on the White House TikTok post. Representatives for Kahan and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Kahan joins a growing list of artists, including Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter, who have publicly condemned the administration for using their music in unauthorized political and military-related social media content.

This past weekend, Katy Perry blasted the administration for using her 2010 hit "Firework" to soundtrack military strikes. Perry wrote on X that she was "deeply appalled and angry" regarding the unauthorized use.
title: Noah Kahan hits Trump over use of song in social post: ‘Would never approve’

summary: On Monday, United States District Judge John F. Walter sentenced Ismael Vega, 42, of the Westlake neighborhood to 37 months in federal prison for throwing rocks and ignited debris at California Highway Patrol officers during a June 2025 violent protest.

During the evening of June 8, 2025, two days after violence erupted during immigration enforcement protests, Vega joined a large group of protesters on the Main Street overpass above the 101 Freeway in downtown Los Angeles.

In his plea agreement, Vega admitted dropping burning cardboard onto a CHP vehicle and throwing rocks at officers below, acknowledging the debris created substantial risk of death or serious bodily injury. Judge Walter ordered $253,415 in restitution.

Vega is the fifth defendant sentenced in the case. Co-defendant Yachua Mauricio Flores, 23, faces sentencing August 3, while lead defendant Adam Charles Palermo, 40, is scheduled for December 14 and faces up to 20 years in prison.

Prosecutors noted the incident "stood apart in its magnitude," as a California Highway Patrol sergeant with nearly 30 years of law enforcement experience described the profound, lasting impact the violent civil disorder had on both him and his son.
title: Man sentenced for throwing rocks, burning debris at CHP officers during L.A. protest

summary: On Wednesday, Sen. Jacky Rosen secured unanimous consent for a resolution opposing clemency for Ghislaine Maxwell , with every Senate Republican supporting the measure without objection.

President Donald Trump's repeated refusal to rule out exercising his pardoning power prompted the resolution; he previously told reporters at his Turnberry resort in Scotland he was 'allowed to give her a pardon.'

Epstein survivor Dani Bensky testified during Senate Judiciary Committee hearings that Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche spent nine hours interviewing Maxwell but 'did not even spend nine minutes meeting with a survivor.'

Simultaneously, U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan ordered Blanche to deliver unredacted Epstein-related documents to his chambers by 3 p.m. on the same day as the committee vote, intensifying scrutiny.

While the resolution is nonbinding, its unanimous passage demonstrates significant bipartisan pushback against potential executive action on accountability for crimes involving sexual exploitation of children.
title: Senate unanimously agrees to oppose pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell

summary: On Tuesday, the Jackson County Chancery Court issued subpoenas to Life360, Snap, Meta , TikTok, and WhatsApp at the request of Nolan Wells' mother, requiring the companies to preserve and produce digital records within 21 days.

The legal action follows Wells' disappearance on the Fourth of July during a boat trip to Horn Island; he was found dead two days later, with an independent autopsy listing his cause of death as undetermined.

Seeking clarity, the family's legal team aims to recover potentially deleted metadata and location logs after Christine Wonsley reported finding no recent activity on her son's phone despite his frequent social media usage.

As local authorities prepare to turn findings over to a grand jury, the case has drawn national attention, prompting leaders including Rev. Al Sharpton and filmmaker Tyler Perry to offer a combined $100,000 reward for information.

Conflicting reports regarding the circumstances of Wells' death have fueled the family's demand for transparency, as they continue to challenge early characterizations and pursue a thorough investigation.
title: Nolan Wells' mother subpoenas social media, tech companies seeking answers in her son's death

With the latest strikes dashing hopes for a return to negotiations, resistance groups warned that hostilities would persist, stating, "As long as the threats against the Islamic Republic of Iran continue...the resistance will continue.
title: US Military Launches 'Powerful' Retaliatory Strikes on Iran

summary: On Tuesday, a hammer-wielding man entered the Lev Leviev School in Forest Hills and shoved an 8-year-old child into a fence, causing a head injury. Camp counselors and security subdued the suspect before police arrived and took him into custody.

Law-Enforcement sources confirmed the suspect has an extensive criminal history with dozens of prior arrests and documented mental-health incidents. Police are investigating whether the assault was motivated by antisemitic bias, though no motive has yet been established.

This incident follows a stabbing last week on Manhattan's Upper West Side where witnesses alleged the attacker shouted "Allahu Akbar" during the assault. The series of attacks has left many Jewish New Yorkers increasingly fearful.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces intensified scrutiny over his relationship with the Jewish community following the violence. Moshe Spern, president of United Jewish Teachers, warned that "inflammatory rhetoric" from Mamdani could "incite further hostility or targeting of Jewish institutions."

Anti-Jewish offenses dominated New York City's hate-crime statistics during the first half of 2026. The NYPD recorded 178 confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes, accounting for 55.3 percent of all citywide hate crimes despite Jews comprising roughly 10 percent of the population.
title: Report on Jewish diaspora finds biggest rise in antisemitism in UK

summary: On Tuesday, Jonathan Veitch, head of UNICEF for the Palestinian territories, reported that Israeli water infrastructure restrictions are squandering Canadian aid, citing destruction of the Canada Well facility.

Israel restricts items like cement and generators as 'dual-use' materials to prevent Hamas from building weapons, forcing UNICEF to become the 'provider of last resort' for water and sanitation services across Gaza.

Veitch described dire conditions where families live in makeshift tents surrounded by waste, with nighttime temperatures seldom dropping below 25 C and "millions and millions of rats" infesting the area.
The Israeli Defense Forces stated last week it is assessing infrastructure damage with severity, while 2.1 million Gazans remain confined to 30 per cent of the territory facing critical shortages.

Canada "punches above its weight" in humanitarian assistance, Veitch said, noting private donations helped end a recent famine, though he warned peace remains elusive as thousands grow up without education.
title: UNICEF Official Says Gaza Water Restrictions Waste Canadian Aid

summary: Overnight on July 29, the QatarEnergy-controlled LNG tanker Al Areesh exited the Strait of Hormuz, bound for Port Qasim, Pakistan, marking the first such departure visible on ship-tracking data since July 11.
The departure follows the early July strike on the Al Rekayyat, which halted QatarEnergy-controlled LNG transits; the Al Hamra was the last tanker to exit on July 11 before this three-week pause.

Meanwhile, the ADNOC Gas-controlled Mraweh LNG tanker reappeared inside the strait on Thursday after last being detected outside on July 24, while 12 commodity ships transited the waterway on Wednesday with six entering and six exiting.
Separately, visible crude loadings from the Red Sea port of Yanbu fell by at least 30% last week after Yemen's Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia, disrupting regional energy flows.

Vortexa analyst George Morris noted that cargoes loaded at Yanbu accounted for "around 15% of Asia 's seaborne crude/condensate imports in June," while unreported 'dark' tanker activity complicates full assessment of supply chain disruptions.
title: QatarEnergy buys 33 US LNG cargoes to offset Hormuz disruption

summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani expressed openness to slavery reparations and highlighted the city's complicity in slavery beyond typical geographic perceptions.
The New York City Commission on Racial Equity was created in 2024 to study the city's role in slavery and its legacies, with reports on reparations due in 2027 and implementation expected by 2028.
CORE has engaged thousands of New Yorkers, allocated $500,000 to community groups for reparations discussions, and organized events like the largest Juneteenth reparations gathering.
There are concerns that reparations efforts may face federal legal challenges, referencing past Justice Department interventions against racially focused programs.
title: Mamdani signals he is open to slavery reparations

summary: On Wednesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed proposals to restrict oil exports to the United States as a trade bargaining chip, warning such actions would undermine Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier.
Last week, Ontario Premier Doug Ford proposed leveraging critical energy exports to "dismantle" the United States in response to Washington's threatened round of tariffs.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose province supplies most Canadian oil to the United States, also opposes curbing exports, while Carney emphasized that "the best" commodity Canada offers is trust.
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he does not care about renewing the free trade deal, while threatening additional punitive measures later this month.
Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charette are in Washington today negotiating as the Trump administration prepares to implement 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods on August 19.
title: Carney plays down idea of curbing Canadian oil supplies to US amid trade war
